ask_what_it_is.notes: Prove something is actually answering before asking it for anything. A socket file existing says only that a path exists; an answer says a container engine is running behind it.

list_what_it_can_run.notes: The images this engine already holds. Reading this before building tells you whether the thing you were about to make is already there.

look_closely_at_one_thing_it_can_run.notes: What a built artifact actually IS, which is not what you asked for until you check. A build reuses cached layers, so asking for one architecture and receiving another is quiet and only shows up where the thing is meant to run. Read Architecture and Os back before sending it anywhere.

build_something_it_can_run.notes: Make a runnable artifact out of a folder. The body is the FOLDER, not a description of it, which is what body_encoding folder-as-a-tar means: the whole folder is packed and sent, deterministically, so the same folder always produces the same bytes and therefore the same content address. which_architecture matters and has no safe default: this machine is arm64 and the machines this is usually built FOR are amd64, so building without saying so produces something that will not run where it is going and says nothing about it until then. The answer is a stream of progress lines rather than one object, so read the last lines for the outcome.

payload.notes: The second way of reaching, and it arrived the way this system said it would. A note declared a reach the one performer could not do, the performer REFUSED it whole rather than half-following it, and that refusal was the request for a capability. Some things answer HTTP on a unix socket rather than a host, and a container engine is the one that forced it, because producing an artifact for a host that is not this computer needs one and nothing else could reach it. The socket path is NOT here on purpose: that is a fact about this machine, not about the thing being reached, so the note names the ROLE it needs through reach_through_a_connection_that_fills and machine-wide host DATA says which connection fills it and where it is. Until 2026-09-09 the note named the CONNECTION, which was the same defect one level up, since a connection name is also a fact about one machine; the customer-set text guard caught it on the ship path. Same split as a secret, which a note also names without holding. The host part of these addresses is a placeholder because a socket has no host to resolve; only the path travels. Building arrived the same way the socket reach did: the note asked for a body that is a whole folder, the builder could encode only JSON or a form, and its own docstring already said new encodings are added there as capabilities keyed by DATA rather than as a per-thing branch. So folder-as-a-tar is now one encoding that serves anything wanting a folder, not a container-specific path.

list_machines.notes: What is running, and on which image. Read this before changing anything, because the image you are replacing is the one you roll back to.

read_machine.notes: One machine, including its full current config. The config you get back is the shape you hand to change_what_a_machine_runs, so read it, change the one field, and send it back.

create_machine.notes: Start a new machine in an app from a whole config (image, guest size, metadata). The answer is the machine, with its id. Read list_machines first: a machine is billed from the moment it exists.

destroy_machine.notes: Remove one machine, stopping it first. Read it first and check it is the one you mean: removal cannot be undone, and its volume is left behind (list_storage_volumes).

change_what_a_machine_runs.notes: Make a machine run a different prepared artifact. This is the whole of 'deploy' once the artifact exists: producing the artifact belongs to whatever owns artifacts, and this owns only making the target run it. The whole config is ONE fact because you read it back first and change one field, which is also why rolling back is the same ask with the previous image. It is not a hand deploy: it is a declared operation on a package note, which is exactly the path the agent guard points at instead of a typed command.

wait_for_a_machine_to_be_ready.notes: Answer only once the machine reaches the state asked for, so a change is proven rather than assumed. A deploy that returns before the target is serving has proven nothing.

list_storage_volumes.notes: Every storage volume and what it is attached to. The reason this exists next to list_machines: a volume OUTLIVES the machine that used it, so a machine listing showing nothing says nothing about what is still being billed. Each answer carries whether a volume is attached, which is the only fact needed to tell a volume in use from one nobody can reach.

read_storage_volume.notes: One volume, including its size and attachment. Read this before destroying anything, for the same reason read_machine comes before changing one: the thing you are removing is the thing you cannot put back by asking again.

extend_storage_volume.notes: Grow one volume. This sat missing next to list, read and destroy, and the shape of that gap is worth naming: the connection could DELETE storage and could not GROW it, so the only reachable answer to a full volume was a destructive one. A full volume does not announce itself either. The app stopped booting with no error line at all, because the step that writes simply could not, and the only visible evidence was a block count in a filesystem check line that reads as routine boot noise. Growing is not recoverable in the way destroying is, and in the opposite direction: a provider will usually not shrink a volume back, so every use of this is a standing cost until somebody moves the data. Read the volume first and say what made the current size wrong, because a volume that filled once will fill again and the size is a symptom of what is being kept, never the fix for it.

destroy_storage_volume.notes: Remove a volume nobody is attached to. Destructive and deliberately named as such. The provider keeps its own snapshot for a retention window, which is what makes this recoverable rather than final, and that window is the provider's fact and not ours to assume: read it from the volume rather than trusting a number written here. Pairs with list_storage_volumes, never with a name or a guess, because the only safe input is a volume the provider itself reports as unattached.

kinds_it_holds.notes: Every kind of thing this connection can be holding that keeps costing until somebody removes it, and which ask enumerates each. A sweep walks THIS list rather than the asks, so a kind with no ask is a loud row saying so instead of silence, where a kind nobody asks about and a kind with nothing in it otherwise produce the identical answer. This exists because a sweep built the obvious way on a connection reports only on kinds somebody already thought to declare a request for, and this one had machine requests and no volume request for as long as it existed. It is NOT the reason a storage volume once billed for a month: the separate weekly script that found that one could see volumes perfectly well and ended its report by telling a person to go and destroy it. Blindness and a human cron are two different failures and only one of them is fixed here. Adding a kind is one row; giving it an ask is one row in instrument_requests. Rows say `what` rather than `kind`, because `kind` names a RECORD KIND everywhere else in this corpus and reusing it would claim an identity in that shared namespace for something that is not a record at all.

where_this_list_came_from.why_this_is_marked: which kinds a provider bills for is the PROVIDER'S fact and they add to it without telling us, so this is a snapshot with a hidden expiry (L216). It is marked rather than trusted, so a sweep can list every hand-typed list and its date instead of a reader assuming this was current.

when_nobody_is_using_one.notes: A volume outlives the machine that used it, so nothing about a machine listing says whether this is still wanted. Attachment is the whole of the question and the provider answers it directly.

rules.label: The provider keeps a snapshot of it after removal

only_when_this_is_readable_first.why: Removing this is recoverable only for as long as the provider keeps its own snapshot, and how long that is belongs to them and changes without telling us. Reading it off the very thing about to be removed is the difference between a recoverable act and one that reads recoverable in a file written months ago. A volume that will not say is not eligible. It says WHAT THE ANSWER MUST PROVE rather than which field must be there, and that is the whole of the difference: the field-presence version accepted a retention of 0, which is the provider saying it keeps nothing, and a retention of "not-a-duration", which is nobody being able to tell, as proof that destroying it was recoverable.

payload.notes: This note owns HALF of a deploy, and saying which half is the point. A deploy is two halves: produce an artifact, then cause a target to run it. This note owns the second half only. It can move a machine onto an artifact that already exists, and it cannot bring one into being. The second half belongs here because it is an instance of reaching an outside thing and asking it to change state, which this file already owns for every other outside thing, so a deploy-shaped package would have been a second copy of this mechanism wearing a vendor's name. Nothing here is Fly-specific except the addresses, which are DATA: another host with an HTTP API is another row in this file and no code anywhere changes, which is the provider-neutral deployment algebra rather than a promise of one. The agent guard forbids a HAND deploy, meaning a typed command with no owner; this is the declared operation it points at instead. MEASURED 2026-09-04: nothing in the package set produced a container image, a sweep for Dockerfile, docker build, buildpack and oci-archive returned zero producers, and the missing piece was named exactly, a sibling container-image row on the generic artifact owner native-artifact, where macOS is one named artifact kind rather than a branch. ✅ THAT HALF NOW EXISTS, 2026-09-20: native-artifact/do-work/project-container-image-layer.mjs reads the same file manifests the other artifact kinds read, selects by output prefix, reports every unselected entry rather than dropping it, and stops at a build context, which the generic deployment owner then deploys. The prediction written here held, so the sentence is kept rather than replaced: it is the record of a gap being named before it was filled. What this note says about ITSELF is unchanged and still the point: it moves a machine onto an artifact and cannot bring one into being, so the two halves stay separate owners.

start_exchange.notes: Places one outbound call. CORRECTED 2026-09-04: this used to say the brain is ours because an agent created with voiceMode webhook posts caller speech to our own webhook. That describes a configuration nobody had created, and it made this note read as unusable for four hours. What is true: when `spoken_task` is supplied, the carrier runs the model against OUR wording regardless of the agent's inbound voice mode, and returns the transcript after the call. So the wording and the transcript are ours and the model is theirs. Webhook mode is still the target, so that the model is ours too, and it needs a publicly reachable turn route that does not exist yet.
start_exchange.two_field_names_here_were_wrong_from_the: It sent `to` and `from`. The carrier takes `toNumber` and `fromNumberId`, so every call this note could have placed would have failed on a malformed body. Nobody found it because the note was never RUN, only read, and a note that has never been executed is a hypothesis wearing the shape of an owner. `metadata` was dropped in the same pass: it is not a documented field on this endpoint, and sending an undocumented key is guessing with extra steps.
start_exchange.why_spoken_task_is_the_field_that_matter: Without it the carrier falls back to whatever the referenced agent was configured with, which on this account is the vendor's website demo script. With it the carrier runs OUR wording and needs no webhook, which is the documented autonomous mode and works regardless of the agent's inbound voice mode. It is marked optional because the carrier treats it as optional, not because a call is worth placing without it: a call with no spoken_task is a demo bot talking to a stranger. What keeps the dealer, the vehicle and the objective out of this note is that the substitution NAMES here are generic and their VALUES arrive at the moment of the call, from workflow inputs when an engine is serving and from --text-fact through the one door when none is. CORRECTED 2026-09-04: this sentence used to say 'the exchange profile supplies it', which named a stored record that does not exist. Searched all 309 packages that day: spoken_task appears in exactly one file, this one. That is the same defect this note already records twice about itself, a hypothesis wearing the shape of an owner, committed a third time by the note about its own supplier. A stored campaign record would be a real improvement, because six calls sharing one objective currently retype it six times, but it has to be built before it can be cited.

turn_the_opening_code_into_a_session.notes: The code handed back when the account opened is NOT a session and is refused as one. It is swapped here for the session everything else carries. Proven live 2026-09-03.

who_am_i.notes: An ordinary authenticated read, not part of opening the account. It was written carrying the signup session in its own Authorization header, which made it the one operation here that could never run once the account existed. The key arrives through credential_injections like every other authenticated ask.

payload.notes: A carrier that can carry our wording and return the transcript when spoken_task is supplied. Opening the account needed no card and no browser: a code to a mailbox, and we owned a mailbox. HISTORICAL PRE-FUNDING MEASUREMENT 2026-09-04: read_money_left returned used=1, limit=49, remaining=48, but start_exchange returned HTTP 402, 'Add funds on the Billing page to place outbound calls.' That number quota was not spendable calling credit. After a $10 top-up covered by the account owner's standing approval later that day, generic start_exchange and read_exchange completed two real outbound calls and returned transcripts; paid recording stayed disabled. Do not infer free outbound calling or a current balance from the usage quota: billing funds are spend-limit DATA read through the vendor billing surface.

made_at.label: Spotify for Developers
steps: Open the Spotify for Developers dashboard and sign in with a Spotify Premium account (Spotify requires Premium for an app's owner).
Click Create app, name it Trillion, add the redirect address shown above as a Redirect URI, tick Web API and save.
Open the app's Settings and copy the Client ID and Client secret into the boxes below, then click Save.
Until Spotify grants extended access (it asks for an organisation with 250,000 monthly users), only up to 5 people added under User Management can sign in.

acquire.notes: Spotify Authorization Code with PKCE. Since 2024-11-27 new apps cannot read audio features or audio analysis, so Trillion reads what is playing and its cover, and hears the music itself from the computer or the room. Since 2026-03-09 an app in development mode needs a Premium owner and allows 5 people. Read 2026-10-04 from developer.spotify.com and TechCrunch 2026-02-06.

read_usage.notes: What a Cloudflare account used between two days (UTC, inclusive): Worker requests and CPU time, Durable Object requests, running time and rows read and written, Workers AI neurons, KV operations by kind, and R2 operations by kind and bytes kept, from Cloudflare's own analytics. Reads only.

read_store_health.notes: How a Cloudflare account's stores and pages did over the last 24 hours and the 24 hours before them, from Cloudflare's own analytics: each Durable Object that was restarted for running out of memory (namespace, object, how many times), and the first-paint time (median and 75th percentile, in microseconds) of the pages on one host at the paths given, from Cloudflare Web Analytics. The window ends when the read runs. Reads only.

host.description: The host whose pages' first paint is read, like app.example.com.

paths.description: The paths on that host to read, like ["/", "/home"].

read_usage_by_hour.notes: What a Cloudflare account used between two days (UTC, inclusive), hour by hour, from Cloudflare's own analytics: the 1000 Durable Object hours that wrote the most rows and the 1000 that read the most (each object's rows read and written), and the 1000 Worker hours with the most requests (requests and CPU time), so Spend can show which store or Worker used what and when while the answer stays small. Reads only.
